about.heading: The question
paragraphs: Erdős asked whether $\sum_{a\in A}1/(2^a-1)$ is irrational for every infinite set $A$ of positive integers. The question is open. The papers here prove that the sum is irrational when $A$ satisfies a weighted summability condition, when $A$ has a summable divisor cover, and when $A$ lies in the union of a set of each kind. Each result holds with any integer $b\ge2$ in place of $2$. The simplest case is the one Erdős stated in 1968: every infinite $A$ with $\sum_{a\in A}1/a<\infty$.

Erdős proved the case of all positive integers in 1948, and in 1968 the case of pairwise coprime sets with finite reciprocal sum, remarking without details that coprimality could be removed. Duverney and Tachiya proved the squarefree case, and Tao and Teräväinen the case of the primes.

about.heading: What was asked, what is proved and what stays open
paragraphs: Is $X_A(2)=\sum_{a\in A}1/(2^a-1)$ irrational for every infinite set $A$ of positive integers? This is Erdős problem #257. Yes when $\sum_{a\in A}1/a$ is finite, at every integer base $b\ge2$ (short paper, Theorem A.1). Erdős stated this in 1968 without details. More generally, yes when $\sum_{a\in A}h(a)/\bigl(a(2^{h(a)}-1)\bigr)$ is finite, where $h(a)$ is the part of $a$ built from a fixed finite set of primes (Theorem 1.2). Some sets with finite weighted sum have divergent $\sum_{a\in A}1/a$. Arbitrary infinite $A$ stays open: the conditions are sufficient, and none of them characterises the sets in the problem.

Does the joint divisibility of the exponents give irrationality where the weighted condition fails? Yes. If $A$ lies in a union of finite sets $F_j$ for which fractional powers of the divisor counts are bounded by positive divisor sums of summable total cost, then $X_A(b)$ is irrational for every integer $b\ge2$ (Theorem 3.1). Neither condition implies the other (Proposition 5.1), and they combine: every infinite subset of $E\cup V$, with $E$ of the first kind and $V$ of the second, has an irrational sum (Theorem 4.1). Corollary 5.2 exhibits a set that lies in neither class and needs the combined theorem. It has no Lean proof at the revision this reader pins.

Is a prescribed rational number, such as $1/2$ or $1/21$, equal to $X_A(2)$ for some set $A$? For a finite set $F$, the multiplicative order of $b$ modulo the reduced denominator of $X_F(b)$ equals the least common multiple of $F$ (Theorem B.1), so $1/21$ is the sum of no finite set. Theorems C.1 and D.1 to D.3 give tests for membership. The tests decide neither $1/2$ nor $1/21$ for infinite sets.

about.heading: How the proof goes
paragraphs: Compare a multiple of the sum with an integer. For a positive integer $N$, the displacement $\Delta_{b,A}(N)=\sum_{a\in A}(b^{N\bmod a}-1)/(b^a-1)$ equals $(b^N-1)X_A(b)$ minus an integer, and it is positive when $A$ is infinite. If $X_A(b)=p/q$, then $q\,\Delta_{b,A}(N)$ is a positive integer, so $\Delta_{b,A}(N)\ge1/q$. It therefore suffices to find displacements that tend to zero.

Take $N$ to be a multiple of a modulus. When $N$ is a multiple of $Q$, each exponent dividing $Q$ contributes nothing. An exponent that shares a large common divisor with $Q$ has a small mean over a complete period of its residues.

Average over dyadic lengths. The bound for an incomplete period lacks the factor $1/a$. Averaging over the lengths $2^j$ restores it: an exponent enters the truncated error only once the sampled range reaches it, and the reciprocals of the later lengths form a geometric tail bounded by a multiple of $1/a$.

Choose one index. The mean of the displacements over the sampled indices is then small, so some sampled $N$ has $\Delta_{b,A}(N)$ below any prescribed $\varepsilon$. This contradicts $\Delta_{b,A}(N)\ge1/q$. Both criteria use the same average, so for a union one index makes both errors small.

about.heading: Theorem A.1, clause by clause
paragraphs: Theorem A.1 of the short paper is the statement Erdős gave in 1968. Its Lean statement is irrational_erdosSupportSeries_of_summable_reciprocal, which also allows the set to contain 0. The exposition proves the theorem at base two only, so the Lean statement says more than the exposition's Theorem 1 in the base as well. An AI agent compared the clauses, and no independent mathematician has reviewed the comparison.

The base and the set, $b\ge2$ and $A$ infinite (Lean: (b : ℕ) (A : Set ℕ) (hb : 2 ≤ b) (hA : A.Infinite)): the Lean says more. The Lean allows $A$ to contain $0$, which the paper excludes. Lean's division by $0$ gives $0$, so the exponent $0$ adds $0$ to both sums, and on sets of positive integers the two statements agree. The exposition's Theorem 1 fixes $b=2$.
The condition $\sum_{a\in A}1/a<\infty$ (Lean: hsum : Summable (reciprocalSupportTerm A)): the same. reciprocalSupportTerm A takes the value $1/a$ at $a$ in $A$ and $0$ elsewhere.

The conclusion, $X_A(b)=\sum_{a\in A}1/(b^a-1)$ is irrational (Lean: Irrational (erdosSupportSeries b A)): the same. erdosSupportSeries b A is the sum over all natural numbers $a$ of $1/(b^a-1)$ for $a$ in $A$ and $0$ elsewhere.

about.heading: Where the papers and the Lean come from
paragraphs: The papers and the Lean are Will Cook's, from the public repository wcook04/plectis-erdos at one pinned revision. The reading copies are transcribed from the published text by a program, which compares every word with the source and typesets every formula. The PDFs are the published files, unchanged.
Will Cook built and directed the research and reviewed the claims when he could. AI agents did most of the research, the drafting and the Lean. No independent mathematician has reviewed the papers.

about.heading: What a link between a paper and the Lean means
paragraphs: Most links from a printed result to its Lean declaration are copied from the evidence record that the papers themselves publish. The others were written for this reader by an AI agent that read both sides. The reader says which kind each link is.

A link says where to look. A program confirms that both ends exist in the pinned files. Whether the paper's sentence and the Lean statement mean the same is a reading, recorded with the name of who made it, and no independent mathematician has reviewed these readings.

about.heading: What was run
paragraphs: The Lean was compiled and compared by public GitHub Actions runs in the source repositories, and this reader records those runs with their outcomes, failures included. Nothing was compiled again for this reader, and the statuses it shows are the ones those runs recorded.
